claim: Sustained TNF-α stimulation induces transcriptional memory dependent on TET enzymes in HEK293F cells.
source: Using HEK293F cells as a model system, we report that sustained TNF-α stimulation induces transcriptional memory dependent on TET enzymes.
evidence: The abstract directly states this finding, which is supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript showing TET enzyme requirement for transcriptional memory.

claim: The hypomethylated status of transcriptional regulatory regions can be inherited, facilitating NF-κB binding and more robust subsequent activation.
source: The hypomethylated status of transcriptional regulatory regions can be inherited, facilitating NF-κB binding and more robust subsequent activation.
evidence: This claim is supported by bisulfite sequencing data showing maintained demethylation after TNF-α withdrawal and ChIP-seq data showing enhanced p65 binding.

claim: A high initial methylation level and CpG density around κB sites are correlated with the functional potential of transcriptional memory modules.
source: A high initial methylation level and CpG density around κB sites are correlated with the functional potential of transcriptional memory modules.
evidence: This is supported by genome-wide analysis showing correlation between initial methylation/CpG density and memory gene characteristics (Figure 6).

claim: The CALCB gene exhibits the best transcriptional memory among identified genes.
source: Interestingly, the CALCB gene, encoding the proven migraine therapeutic target CGRP, exhibits the best transcriptional memory.
evidence: RNA-seq data shows CALCB has the highest fold-change in second induction compared to first induction (Figure 2B).

claim: A neighboring primate-specific endogenous retrovirus stimulates more rapid, more strong, and at least 100-fold more sensitive CALCB induction in subsequent TNF-α stimulation.
source: A neighboring primate-specific endogenous retrovirus stimulates more rapid, more strong, and at least 100-fold more sensitive CALCB induction in subsequent TNF-α stimulation.
evidence: This is supported by ERV deletion experiments, dose-response experiments showing 125-fold increased sensitivity, and evolutionary conservation analysis.

claim: TNF-α-mediated transcriptional memory greatly sensitizes memory genes to much lower doses of inflammatory cues.
source: Our study reveals that TNF-α-mediated transcriptional memory is governed by active DNA demethylation and greatly sensitizes memory genes to much lower doses of inflammatory cues.
evidence: Dose-response experiments show memory-consolidated cells respond to 0.4 ng/mL TNF-α as well as naive cells respond to 50 ng/mL (Figure 7A).

claim: The CMV promoter contains several κB sites.
source: Because the CMV promoter contains several κB sites (Figure 1A), we took advantage of the reporter cells and examined whether TNF-α treatment could activate the reporter gene and even induce transcriptional memory.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1A schematic.

claim: TNF-α treatment gradually potentiated the expression capacity of the EGFP reporter over time.
source: We first treated the reporter cells naïve to TNF-α with 50 ng/mL TNF-α (this concentration applies to all of the following experiments, unless indicated otherwise) for various lengths of time (Figure 1B), and the percentages of EGFP-positive cells were 0.96% (0 day), 43.7% (2 day), 56.3% (4 days), 69.0% (8 days), and 79.5% (12 days) (Figure 1C).
evidence: Flow cytometry data shows increasing percentages of EGFP-positive cells with longer TNF-α treatment.

claim: Cells that had experienced longer initial TNF-α treatment exhibited much more robust EGFP expression during second induction.
source: Apparently, cells that had experienced longer initial TNF-α treatment exhibited much more robust EGFP expression, and EGFP-positive cells were 13.8% (0 day pretreatment), 18.6% (2 days pretreatment), 25.6% (4 days pretreatment), 40.1% (8 days pretreatment), and 56.5% (12 days pretreatment) of total cells (Figure 1D).
evidence: Flow cytometry data shows dose-dependent increase in EGFP expression during second induction based on duration of first induction.

claim: Sufficient time during the initial induction phase is needed to consolidate transcriptional memory.
source: These data indicate that not all initial TNF-α treatments were equal in inducing inflammatory transcriptional memory, and sufficient time was needed during the initial induction phase to consolidate transcriptional memory.
evidence: This is inferred from the time-course experiments showing stronger memory effects with longer initial TNF-α treatment.

claim: TNF-α treatment induces gradual demethylation of the CMV promoter.
source: We then exposed naïve cells to TNF-α treatment for various lengths of time and measured the CMV promoter methylation levels, giving the following results: 90.6% (0 day), 86.1% (2 days), 76.7% (4 days), 56.7% (8 days), and 41.7% (12 days) (Figure 1F).
evidence: Bisulfite sequencing data shows progressive decrease in methylation with longer TNF-α treatment.

claim: CMV promoter methylation levels are maintained after 10 days of TNF-α withdrawal.
source: Importantly, the CMV promoter methylation levels of cells experiencing different durations of TNF-α treatment were still maintained after 10 days of TNF-α withdrawal (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Bisulfite sequencing data after recovery period shows maintained demethylation.

claim: TNF-α-induced CMV promoter demethylation mainly depends on TET2, with some contribution of TET3 and little participation of TET1.
source: Obviously, TNF-α-induced CMV promoter demethylation mainly depended on TET2, with some contribution of TET3 and little participation of TET1 (Figure 1G).
evidence: Bisulfite sequencing of sorted cells from TET1 KO, TET2 KO, TET3 KO, and TET TKO cells shows differential effects.

claim: TET enzyme-mediated DNA demethylation is required for the optimal activation and inflammatory transcriptional memory of the CMV reporter.
source: These data demonstrate that TET enzyme–mediated DNA demethylation is required for the optimal activation and inflammatory transcriptional memory of the CMV reporter.
evidence: TET2 KO and TET TKO cells show impaired EGFP expression and memory effects (Figure 1H, I).

claim: Five endogenous genes together with the EGFP reporter were defined as inflammatory transcriptional memory genes.
source: Among them, five endogenous genes together with the EGFP reporter were defined as inflammatory transcriptional memory genes, as they were expressed at least 1.3-fold higher in the second TNF-α induction than in the first TNF-α induction and exhibited an FPKM (fragments per kilobase of transcript per million mapped fragments) value greater than 5 (Figure 2B).
evidence: RNA-seq data comparing first and second induction identifies genes meeting defined criteria.

claim: EGFP, CALCB, and PTGES displayed excellent memory effects, whereas the memory effects of CCL2, TNF, and LHX2 were relatively moderate.
source: The EGFP reporter and five endogenous memory genes can be categorized into two groups: EGFP, CALCB, and PTGES displayed excellent memory effects, whereas the memory effects of CCL2, TNF, and LHX2 were relatively moderate (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: RNA-seq data shows differential magnitude of memory effects among identified genes.

claim: EGFP, CALCB, and PTGES displayed apparently elevated baseline expression in the absence of TNF-α signal after the initial induction.
source: Indeed, EGFP, CALCB, and PTGES also displayed apparently elevated baseline expression in the absence of TNF-α signal after the initial induction (Figure 2C).
evidence: RNA-seq data comparing expression after recovery period to naive cells.

claim: IL32 was upregulated in cells with 12-day TNF-α pretreatment but did not exhibit a stronger second induction.
source: IL32 was upregulated in cells with 12-day TNF-α pretreatment (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A; Zhao et al., 2019), but IL32 did not exhibit a stronger second induction (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: RNA-seq data shows IL32 behavior differs from memory genes despite being TNF-α responsive.

claim: CALCB encodes β-CGRP.
source: Second, CALCB encodes β-CGRP.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the CALCB gene.

claim: β-CGRP and α-CGRP (encoded by CALCA) are two isoforms of CGRP that are 37-amino acid secreted neuropeptides and differ by three amino acids in humans.
source: β-CGRP, and α-CGRP (encoded by CALCA) are two isoforms of CGRP (calcitonin gene-related peptide). They are 37-amino acid–secreted neuropeptides and differ by three amino acids in humans (Russell et al., 2014; Russo, 2015).
evidence: This is cited knowledge from published literature.

claim: The two CGRP isoforms share similar biological activities and are potent vasodilators.
source: The two CGRP isoforms share similar biological activities and are potent vasodilators (Brain et al., 1985; Russell et al., 2014).
evidence: This is cited knowledge from published literature.

claim: The overexpression of CGRP is an important cause of migraine.
source: The overexpression of CGRP is an important cause of migraine (Edvinsson et al., 2018; Ho et al., 2010; Pellesi et al., 2017; Russell et al., 2014; Russo, 2015; Tepper, 2018)
evidence: This is cited knowledge from multiple published studies.

claim: Several monoclonal antibodies (eptinezumab, fremanezumab, galcanezumab, and erenumab) against CGRP or CGRP receptors have been approved by the FDA as therapeutics for migraine patients.
source: and several monoclonal antibodies (eptinezumab, fremanezumab, galcanezumab, and erenumab) against CGRP or CGRP receptors have been approved by the FDA as therapeutics for migraine patients.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about FDA-approved therapeutics.

claim: CALCB gene expression reached very high levels with an average FPKM value of 699 after 12 days of TNF-α treatment and 346 after 12 hr of TNF-α treatment in cells with 12 days of prior TNF-α exposure.
source: We noticed that CALCB gene expression reached very high levels in some conditions we analyzed, with an average FPKM value of 699 after 12 days of TNF-α treatment and 346 after 12 hr of TNF-α treatment in cells with 12 days of prior TNF-α exposure (Figure 2D).
evidence: RNA-seq data quantifies CALCB expression levels under different conditions.

claim: CALCB exhibited robust induction with faster kinetics and stronger expression during subsequent induction.
source: We then measured CALCB induction kinetics in cells with or without prior TNF-α exposure, and clearly, CALCB exhibited robust induction with faster kinetics and stronger expression during subsequent induction (Figure 2E).
evidence: RT-qPCR time-course data comparing first and second induction.

claim: The transcriptional memory effect of CALCB was maintained for at least 30 days in the absence of TNF-α.
source: Importantly, the transcriptional memory effect of CALCB was maintained for at least 30 days in the absence of TNF-α (Figure 2F).
evidence: RT-qPCR data after 30-day recovery period shows maintained memory effect.

claim: The transcriptomes of the naïve cells and memory consolidated cells were extremely similar (r = 0.999).
source: Importantly, the transcriptomes of the naïve cells and memory consolidated cells were extremely similar (r = 0.999), and the same was true for the transcriptomes of the first and second inductions (r = 0.999) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C)
evidence: RNA-seq correlation analysis shows overall transcriptome similarity.

claim: The general physiology of the cells was not altered during memory consolidation, except for genes primed for memory response.
source: indicating that the general physiology of the cells was not altered during memory consolidation, except for genes primed for memory response.
evidence: This is inferred from the high correlation between transcriptomes.

claim: The deletion of the RELA gene severely impaired TNF-α-induced CALCB activation.
source: The deletion of the RELA gene (Zhao et al., 2019), which encodes p65, severely impaired TNF-α-induced CALCB activation (Figure 3A)
evidence: RT-qPCR data comparing WT and RELA KO cells shows impaired CALCB induction.

claim: The deletion of the RELA gene severely impaired the inflammatory transcriptional memory of CALCB.
source: The deletion of the RELA gene (Zhao et al., 2019), which encodes p65, severely impaired TNF-α-induced CALCB activation (Figure 3A) and the inflammatory transcriptional memory of CALCB (Figure 3B).
evidence: RT-qPCR data shows RELA KO cells lack memory effect for CALCB.

claim: The induction and memory effect of secreted β-CGRP at the protein level was abrogated in RELA KO cells.
source: Likewise, the induction and memory effect of secreted β-CGRP at the protein level was abrogated in RELA KO cells (Figure 3C).
evidence: ELISA data measuring CGRP protein levels in culture media.

claim: CALCA is barely transcribed in the experimental system.
source: Since CALCA is barely transcribed (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), we were able to measure β-CGRP secreted in the media by performing sandwich ELISA using antibodies against CGRP.
evidence: RNA-seq data shows very low CALCA expression levels.

claim: CALCB expression increased gradually during TNF-α induction.
source: On the other hand, CALCB expression increased gradually during induction (Figure 3D)
evidence: RT-qPCR time-course data shows progressive increase in CALCB expression.

claim: Cells that had experienced longer initial TNF-α exposure displayed higher CALCB expression with subsequent induction.
source: and cells that had experienced longer initial TNF-α exposure displayed higher expression with subsequent induction (Figure 3E).
evidence: RT-qPCR data comparing second induction after different durations of first induction.

claim: TET2 KO and TET TKO cells displayed great defects in reaching the induction peak of CALCB after 12 days of TNF-α treatment.
source: Indeed, TET2 KO and TET TKO cells displayed great defects in reaching the induction peak after 12 days of TNF-α treatment (Figure 3F)
evidence: RT-qPCR data comparing CALCB expression in WT and TET KO cells.

claim: TET2 KO and TET TKO cells failed to maintain robust transcriptional memory of CALCB during the second round of TNF-α treatment.
source: and failed to maintain robust transcriptional memory during the second round of TNF-α treatment (Figure 3G).
evidence: RT-qPCR data shows impaired memory effect in TET2 KO and TET TKO cells.

claim: DNA demethylation mediated by TET enzymes is critical for the inflammatory transcriptional memory of CALCB.
source: These results clearly indicate that DNA demethylation mediated by TET enzymes is critical for the inflammatory transcriptional memory of CALCB.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the TET KO experiments showing impaired memory.

claim: PTGES encodes prostaglandin E synthase that synthesizes a key inflammatory mediator prostaglandin E2.
source: Another gene with excellent inflammatory transcriptional memory is PTGES (Figure 2B), which encodes prostaglandin E synthase that synthesizes a key inflammatory mediator prostaglandin E2 (Gomez et al., 2013; Jakobsson et al., 1999).
evidence: This is cited knowledge about PTGES gene function.

claim: PTGES reached higher expression during long-term TNF-α induction.
source: Similar to CALCB, PTGES also reached higher expression during long-term TNF-α induction (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: RT-qPCR data shows progressive increase in PTGES expression.

claim: RELA KO disrupted PTGES TNF-α-induced activation and transcriptional memory.
source: and RELA KO disrupted its TNF-α-induced activation and transcriptional memory (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: RT-qPCR data comparing WT and RELA KO cells for PTGES expression.

claim: The elevated expression of all inflammatory transcriptional memory genes during the second TNF-α treatment was abrogated in TET TKO cells.
source: The elevated expression of all inflammatory transcriptional memory genes during the second TNF-α treatment was abrogated in TET TKO cells (Figure 3H).
evidence: RNA-seq data comparing WT and TET TKO cells shows loss of memory effect for all identified genes.

claim: Inflammatory transcriptional memory is controlled by DNA demethylation mediated by TET enzymes.
source: Therefore, we conclude that inflammatory transcriptional memory is controlled by DNA demethylation mediated by TET enzymes.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from multiple experiments showing TET enzyme requirement for memory effects.

claim: The CALCB promoter was unmethylated even in untreated cells.
source: The CALCB promoter was unmethylated even in untreated cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Bisulfite sequencing data shows low methylation at CALCB promoter.

claim: 405 TNF-α-induced p65 peaks were co-occupied by H3K27ac and defined as TNF-α-responsive elements.
source: We identified 405 TNF-α-induced p65 peaks that were co-occupied by H3K27ac (Figure 4A), the best known chromatin indicator of active transcriptional regulatory elements (Creyghton et al., 2010; Heintzman et al., 2009; Zhang et al., 2020), and we defined them as TNF-α-responsive elements.
evidence: ChIP-seq data for p65 and H3K27ac identifies overlapping peaks.

claim: The five endogenous inflammatory transcriptional memory genes were associated with 10 TNF-α-responsive elements.
source: The five endogenous inflammatory transcriptional memory genes were associated with 10 TNF-α-responsive elements (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: ChIP-seq data links p65 peaks to memory genes based on genomic proximity.

claim: Two TNF-α-responsive elements were observed at the upstream distal regions (−10 kb and −3 kb) of CALCB, which are putative enhancers of CALCB.
source: For CALCB, two TNF-α-responsive elements were observed at the upstream distal regions (−10 kb and −3 kb) of CALCB, which we considered putative enhancers of CALCB
evidence: ChIP-seq data identifies p65 and H3K27ac peaks upstream of CALCB.

claim: p65 and H3K27ac exhibited further elevation at TNF-α-responsive elements associated with CALCB and PTGES during second induction.
source: Most importantly, p65 and H3K27ac exhibited further elevation of TNF-α-responsive elements associated with CALCB and PTGES (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: ChIP-seq data comparing first and second induction shows increased signal at these elements.

claim: The two TNF-α-induced enhancers associated with the CALCB gene resided in a 7 kb endogenous retrovirus (ERV) spanning from −10 kb to −3 kb upstream of the transcription start site of CALCB.
source: Interestingly, the two TNF-α-induced enhancers associated with the CALCB gene resided in a 7 kb endogenous retrovirus (ERV) spanning from −10 kb to −3 kb upstream of the transcription start site of CALCB (Figure 4B).
evidence: Genome browser view and repeat element annotation identifies ERV location.

claim: Both MER11B elements contain a κB site flanked by 7 CpG sites within regions spanning approximately 200 bp.
source: Both MER11B elements contain a κB site flanked by 7 CpG sites within regions spanning approximately 200 bp (209 bp for MER11B-left and 166 bp for MER11B-right; Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Sequence analysis identifies κB sites and CpG positions.

claim: Both MER11B regions were highly methylated in cells naïve to TNF-α signaling and became gradually demethylated during TNF-α treatment.
source: We measured the DNA methylation levels of these two regions, and both regions were highly methylated in cells naïve to TNF-α signaling and became gradually demethylated during TNF-α treatment (Figure 4C).
evidence: Bisulfite sequencing data shows progressive demethylation at MER11B elements.

claim: The demethylated states of MER11B elements were well maintained after culturing for 10 days in the absence of TNF-α.
source: The demethylated states were well maintained after culturing for 10 days in the absence of TNF-α (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C)
evidence: Bisulfite sequencing after recovery period shows maintained demethylation.

claim: The demethylated states of MER11B elements could last for 30 days.
source: and could even last for 30 days (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D)
evidence: Bisulfite sequencing after 30-day recovery shows maintained demethylation.

claim: Long-term TNF-α exposure may permanently alter the future signal response in certain cases.
source: indicating that long-term TNF-α exposure, in certain cases, may permanently alter the future signal response.
evidence: This is inferred from the long-lasting demethylation observed at MER11B elements.

claim: TNF-α-induced CALCB enhancer demethylation depended on p65 and the TET enzymes, with a major contribution from TET2.
source: Similar to CMV promoter demethylation, TNF-α-induced CALCB enhancer demethylation depended on p65 and the TET enzymes, with a major contribution from TET2 (Figure 4D).
evidence: Bisulfite sequencing of MER11B elements in RELA KO and TET KO cells shows impaired demethylation.

claim: DNA demethylation occurred at p65 peaks.
source: Indeed, DNA demethylation occurred at p65 peaks (Figure 4E)
evidence: Enzymatic methyl-seq data shows reduced methylation at p65 binding sites.

claim: The demethylation effect was stronger in regions adjacent to the peak centers.
source: and the demethylation effect was stronger in regions adjacent to the peak centers (Figure 4F).
evidence: Methylation analysis relative to p65 binding motif shows position-dependent demethylation.

claim: The deletion of RELA impaired demethylation at p65 peaks.
source: The deletion of RELA impaired the above demethylation events, and the deletion of TET2 reduced the extent of demethylation (Figure 4G).
evidence: Methylation analysis in RELA KO and TET2 KO cells shows reduced demethylation at p65 peaks.

claim: p65 binding per se, but not active transcription, is the main cause of TNF-α-induced demethylation.
source: Therefore, we conclude that p65 binding per se, but not active transcription, is the main cause of TNF-α-induced demethylation, which is in line with an early observation that DNA-binding proteins can induce DNA demethylation without gene activation (Stadler et al., 2011).
evidence: Analysis of p65 peaks grouped by eRNA expression shows similar demethylation regardless of transcriptional activity (Figure 4H).

claim: The activation of CALCB was partially impaired in MER11B-left and MER11B-right KO cells.
source: The activation of CALCB was partially impaired in MER11B-left and MER11B-right KO cells (Figure 5A)
evidence: RT-qPCR data comparing CALCB induction in WT and individual MER11B KO cells.

claim: Both MER11B elements are involved in CALCB activation mediated by TNF-α.
source: suggesting that both MER11B elements were involved in CALCB activation mediated by TNF-α.
evidence: This is inferred from the partial impairment observed in individual MER11B KO cells.

claim: Cells lacking both MER11B elements or the entire ERV completely failed to respond to TNF-α signaling for CALCB activation.
source: On the other hand, cells lacking both MER11B elements or the entire ERV completely failed to respond to TNF-α signaling (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: RT-qPCR data shows no CALCB induction in double MER11B KO and ERV KO cells.

claim: Cells lacking the entire ERV did not display any inflammatory transcriptional memory of CALCB.
source: Cells lacking the entire ERV did not display any inflammatory transcriptional memory of CALCB (Figure 5C)
evidence: RT-qPCR data shows no memory effect in ERV KO cells.

claim: Cells lacking the entire ERV did not display any inflammatory transcriptional memory of secreted β-CGRP.
source: or secreted β-CGRP (Figure 5D).
evidence: ELISA data shows no memory effect for CGRP protein in ERV KO cells.

claim: The CALCB gene is conserved between rodents and humans.
source: Notably, although the CALCB gene is conserved between rodents and humans, this regulatory ERV only exists in some primates (Figure 5E)
evidence: Multiple sequence alignment shows CALCB gene conservation and ERV presence only in primates.

claim: The regulatory ERV associated with CALCB only exists in some primates.
source: Notably, although the CALCB gene is conserved between rodents and humans, this regulatory ERV only exists in some primates (Figure 5E)
evidence: Multiple sequence alignment shows ERV presence only in primate genomes.

claim: The inflammatory transcriptional memory of CALCB emerged during evolution after an ERV was inserted in the neighborhood and this ERV was coopted as the epigenetic memory module.
source: suggesting that the inflammatory transcriptional memory of CALCB emerged during evolution after an ERV was inserted in the neighborhood and that this ERV was coopted as the epigenetic memory module.
evidence: This is inferred from the primate-specific presence of the ERV and its functional requirement for memory.

claim: The p65 peaks associated with the five memory genes were highly methylated in cells naïve to TNF-α and exhibited obvious demethylation during memory consolidation.
source: These peaks displayed several consistent features: they were highly methylated in cells naïve to TNF-α and exhibited obvious demethylation during memory consolidation
evidence: Methylation analysis of the 10 p65 peaks associated with memory genes (Figure 6A).

claim: Demethylation of p65 peaks associated with memory genes was impaired upon the loss of RELA and TET2.
source: their demethylation was impaired upon the loss of RELA and TET2 (Figure 6A)
evidence: Methylation analysis in RELA KO and TET2 KO cells shows reduced demethylation.

claim: p65 peaks associated with memory genes exhibited greater H3K27ac enrichment during the second TNF-α induction.
source: and they exhibited greater H3K27ac enrichment during the second TNF-α induction (Figure 6B).
evidence: ChIP-seq data shows increased H3K27ac signal at these peaks during second induction.

claim: p65 could bind methylated regions but favored unmethylated regions.
source: Indeed, when we grouped p65 peaks according to their initial DNA methylation levels and then plotted p65 occupancy in cells treated with the first dose of TNF-α for 12 hr, it was obvious that p65 could bind methylated regions but favored unmethylated regions (Figure 6C).
evidence: ChIP-seq analysis shows higher p65 occupancy at unmethylated peaks compared to methylated peaks.

claim: One important mechanism in consolidating inflammatory transcriptional memory is to change initially disfavored methylated p65-binding regions into favored unmethylated regions.
source: Thus, one important mechanism in consolidating inflammatory transcriptional memory is to change initially disfavored methylated p65-binding regions into favored unmethylated regions, to facilitate p65 binding and to achieve more effective transcriptional activation when a subsequent stimulus arrives.
evidence: This mechanism is inferred from the observation that p65 favors unmethylated regions and that demethylation occurs during memory consolidation.

claim: The IL32 promoter and CpG islands were demethylated after 12 days of TNF-α treatment.
source: For example, the IL32 promoter and CpG islands were demethylated after 12 days of TNF-α treatment (Zhao et al., 2019)
evidence: This is cited from previous work by the same authors.

claim: The adjacent region of the κB site in the IL32 promoter had fewer CpGs than the other p65 peaks associated with genes displaying a memory effect.
source: To address this critical question, we carefully compared p65 peaks in the IL32 promoter and other transcriptional memory genes, and we noticed that the adjacent region of the κB site in the IL32 promoter had fewer CpGs than the other p65 peaks associated with genes displaying a memory effect (Figure 6D)
evidence: Analysis of CpG numbers around κB sites shows IL32 has fewer CpGs.

claim: The three genes (EGFP, CALCB, and PTGES) with the best memory effects contained more CpGs in their associated p65 peaks.
source: whereas the three genes (EGFP, CALCB, and PTGES) with the best memory effects (Figure 2B) contained more CpGs in their associated p65 peaks (Figure 6D).
evidence: Analysis shows correlation between CpG number and memory effect strength.

claim: p65 occupancy was higher in regions with fewer CpGs even though the methylation levels were equally high.
source: Indeed, p65 occupancy was higher in regions with fewer CpGs even though the methylation levels were equally high (Figure 6E).
evidence: ChIP-seq analysis of methylated peaks grouped by CpG number shows inverse relationship.

claim: The total DNA methylation (combining CpG number and methylation level) in the adjacent regions of κB sites is critical for their potential to serve as epigenetic modules for inflammatory transcriptional memory.
source: The above results suggest that the total DNA methylation (combining CpG number and methylation level) in the adjacent regions of κB sites is critical for their potential to serve as epigenetic modules for inflammatory transcriptional memory.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined analysis of CpG number and methylation level effects.

claim: Regions with higher total methylation were more disfavored for p65 binding.
source: Indeed, when we grouped p65 peaks according to their total methylation level and plotted p65 occupancy in cells treated with the first dose of TNF-α for 12 hr, regions with higher total methylation were clearly more disfavored for p65 binding (Figure 6F).
evidence: ChIP-seq analysis shows inverse relationship between total methylation and p65 occupancy.

claim: The efficiency of methylation-mediated repression depends not only on the methylation level but also on the regional methylated CpG density.
source: In retrospect, this is easy to understand because the efficiency of methylation-mediated repression depends not only on the methylation level but also on the regional methylated CpG density (Curradi et al., 2002; Hsieh, 1994).
evidence: This is cited knowledge from published literature.

claim: Occupancy-increased p65 peaks were prone to high initial methylation and became demethylated after 12 days of TNF-α treatment.
source: We systematically analyzed the occupancy of p65 between the two TNF-α induction times (Figure 6—figure supplement 1) and observed that occupancy-increased peaks were prone to high initial methylation and became demethylated after 12 days of TNF-α treatment (Figure 6G).
evidence: Analysis of p65 occupancy changes shows correlation with initial methylation and demethylation.

claim: The reduction in the number of methylated CpGs promoted p65 binding, chromatin opening, and H3K27ac.
source: We also compared p65 occupancy, ATAC-seq signal, and H3K27ac signal according to various levels of total methylated CpGs, and the reduction in the number of methylated CpGs promoted p65 binding, chromatin opening, and H3K27ac (Figure 6H–J).
evidence: Integrated analysis of ChIP-seq, ATAC-seq, and methylation data shows coordinated changes.

claim: Initially methylated p65 peaks with the largest amount of total demethylation may function as potential inflammatory transcriptional memory modules.
source: The above results suggest that initially methylated p65 peaks with the largest amount of total demethylation may function as potential inflammatory transcriptional memory modules.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between demethylation extent and memory-associated features.

claim: 129 highly demethylated p65 peaks are associated with 106 genes, including all five memory genes.
source: the highly demethylated p65 peaks comprising the top 25% of total demethylation during 12-day TNF-α treatment (129 peaks associated with 106 genes, including all five memory genes)
evidence: Bioinformatic analysis categorizes p65 peaks by demethylation extent and links to genes.

claim: Upon second induction, the genes of the highly demethylated group displayed higher expression of their own enhancer RNAs.
source: First, upon second induction, the genes of the highly demethylated group displayed higher expression of their own enhancer RNAs (Figure 6L).
evidence: RNA-seq analysis of eRNA expression at p65 peaks grouped by demethylation extent.

claim: Neighboring genes associated with the highly demethylated p65 peaks exhibited higher expression during the second induction.
source: Moreover, neighboring genes associated with the highly demethylated p65 peaks also exhibited higher expression during the second induction (Figure 6M).
evidence: RNA-seq analysis of genes near highly demethylated p65 peaks shows increased expression.

claim: The impact on neighboring genes was distance-sensitive, and genes with transcriptional start sites (TSSs) within 10 kb of the highly demethylated p65 peaks exhibited stronger transcriptional memory.
source: In addition, the impact on neighboring genes was distance-sensitive, and genes with transcriptional start sites (TSSs) within 10 kb of the highly demethylated p65 peaks exhibited stronger transcriptional memory (Figure 6N).
evidence: Analysis of gene expression changes grouped by distance to p65 peaks shows distance-dependent effect.

claim: p65 peaks with high initial methylation and CpG density are more likely to serve as inflammatory transcriptional memory modules.
source: Taken together, p65 peaks with high initial methylation and CpG density are more likely to serve as inflammatory transcriptional memory modules.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the integrated analysis of methylation, CpG density, and memory effects.

claim: Cells that had experienced prior TNF-α treatment could achieve an approximately twofold better effect with a 125-fold lower TNF-α concentration (0.4 ng/mL) than naïve cells treated with 50 ng/mL TNF-α.
source: Amazingly, cells that had experienced prior TNF-α treatment could achieve an approximately twofold better effect with a 125-fold lower TNF-α concentration (0.4 ng/mL) than naïve cells treated with 50 ng/mL TNF-α (Figure 7A).
evidence: RT-qPCR data comparing CALCB expression in naive vs. memory-consolidated cells at different TNF-α doses.

claim: This is the first transcriptional memory effect reported to increase signal sensitivity by more than 100-fold.
source: To the best of our knowledge, this is the first transcriptional memory effect reported to increase signal sensitivity by more than 100-fold.
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' knowledge of the literature and their experimental findings.

claim: CALCB and EGFP genes displayed even higher expression in cells with consolidated memory, despite having a 125-fold lower TNF-α signal.
source: Indeed, CALCB and EGFP genes displayed even higher expression in cells with consolidated memory, despite having a 125-fold lower TNF-α signal (Figure 7B).
evidence: RNA-seq data comparing expression at different TNF-α doses in naive vs. memory-consolidated cells.

claim: PTGES reached a 60% expression level in memory consolidated cells treated with a 125-fold lower TNF-α signal, indicating highly improved signal sensitivity.
source: In addition, PEGES reached a 60% expression level in memory consolidated cells treated with a 125-fold lower TNF-α signal (Figure 7B), indicating highly improved signal sensitivity.
evidence: RNA-seq data shows PTGES expression at low TNF-α dose in memory-consolidated cells.

claim: This study clearly demonstrated that TET enzymes are essential in governing transcriptional memory in response to TNF-α, providing a causal role for active DNA demethylation in consolidating transcriptional memory.
source: This study clearly demonstrated that TET enzymes are essential in governing transcriptional memory in response to TNF-α, providing a causal role for active DNA demethylation in consolidating transcriptional memory.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the TET KO experiments showing loss of memory effects.

claim: Sustained inflammatory signals can lead to the formation of transcriptional memory.
source: Our discovery that sustained inflammatory signals can lead to the formation of transcriptional memory and that certain genes under the control of inflammatory transcriptional memory can even increase their sensitivity to inflammatory signals by 100-fold may provide some answers to this long-standing question.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings of the study.

claim: Certain genes under the control of inflammatory transcriptional memory can increase their sensitivity to inflammatory signals by 100-fold.
source: Our discovery that sustained inflammatory signals can lead to the formation of transcriptional memory and that certain genes under the control of inflammatory transcriptional memory can even increase their sensitivity to inflammatory signals by 100-fold may provide some answers to this long-standing question.
evidence: This is based on the dose-response experiments showing >100-fold increased sensitivity.

claim: Signal-induced active DNA demethylation is likely a general principle for transcriptional memory.
source: Our finding of inflammatory signal-induced DNA demethylation and its role in transcriptional memory consolidation is unlikely to be unique to inflammation signaling. We expect this to be an applicable principle for many other types of long-term transcriptional memory.
evidence: This is speculation based on the findings and general principles of transcription factor-induced demethylation.

claim: DNA methylation is likely the best candidate to govern long-term transcriptional memory because it can be maintained for a long time in quiescent cells and can be faithfully inherited for many cell divisions in proliferating cells.
source: In theory, long-term transcriptional memory should be governed by epigenetic mechanisms that can be maintained for a long time in quiescent cells and can be faithfully inherited for many cell divisions in proliferating cells. DNA methylation is likely the best candidate because it meets both criteria.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about DNA methylation stability and the experimental observations of maintained demethylation.

claim: The bimodal behavior of CpG methylation makes it an ideal candidate to store digital information at regulatory regions with a simple status code such as 'naïve/methylated/locked' and 'memory consolidated/unmethylated/unlocked'.
